proposals.evidence: DEDR4395(a) gives Tamil peṇ woman/female, peṇṭu woman/wife, Malayalam peṇ and Kannada peṇṇu/peṇḍa woman. The selected simple southern survey forms are comparative lect extensions within this family; final vowels, gemination and retroflex stops remain as recorded, with no substitution of the marriage sense of other branches. This is a comparative family proposal; inheritance versus local transmission in this survey lect remains subject to review.

proposals.citation: dedr[entry 2248];varghese2015palakkad[Appendix B3, item 87, Malasar, Oriental Estate]
proposals.evidence: DEDR2248 gives Tamil/Malayalam kōḻi fowl, Kota kōy, Kodagu kōḷi, Kannada kōḻi and Tulu kōri/kōḷi. These southern survey kōyi/koyɨ/kōḷi/kośi/kojī-type responses are comparative lect extensions, retaining the glide, lateral and palatal/sibilant variants. The source chicken sense is compatible with fowl; this does not merge them with the distinct central-Dravidian kor family. This is a comparative family proposal; inheritance versus local transmission in this survey lect remains subject to review.

proposals.citation: dedr[entry 4798];varghese2015palakkad[Appendix B3, item 89, Malasar, Oriental Estate]
proposals.evidence: DEDR4798 gives Tamil/Malayalam māṭu ox and Kota māṛ beast, explicitly including cattle and buffalo. The southern survey maḍɨ/maḍu cow responses are comparative lect extensions of this cattle term, with a more specific female-bovine elicitation gloss than the Tamil/Malayalam ox gloss. Preserve that semantic difference and all original vowel-length/voicing notation. This is a comparative family proposal; inheritance versus local transmission in this survey lect remains subject to review.

The selected survey forms preserve their vowel, gemination and voicing variants; Irula/Malasar forms are comparative regional extensions. proposals.citation: dedr[entry 3307];varghese2015palakkad[Appendix B3, item 39, Malasar, Oriental Estate]
proposals.evidence: DEDR3307 gives Tamil/Malayalam/Kodagu tuṇi cloth, with differentiated ritual garment senses in Kota/Toda. These simple southern survey tu ṇi/ṭuṇi/tuṇī cloth responses are comparative lect extensions of the ordinary cloth noun, preserving source-internal spacing and retroflex/vowel notation. The longer tuṇi-maṇi response is excluded pending component analysis. This is a comparative family proposal; inheritance versus local transmission in this survey lect remains subject to review.
